title: Musical chairs in the Senate, Schindler takes up grave matters and new judges, in political notes
summary: Senators reelect Sen. Bill Ferguson as their president for a seventh year and he puts his leadership team in place, former Department of Juvenile Services official Marc Schindler gets a new gig and the governor names four new judges, in political notes.
content:
by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters December 10, 2025

by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters December 10, 2025

If it was supposed to be musical chairs, it was a short song.

Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) announced committee chairs for the 2026 General Assembly, his seventh as president, but most of the faces are familiar to anyone who haunted the Miller Senate Office Building during the 2025 legislative session. That familiarity starts with Ferguson and Senate President Pro Tem Malcolm Augustine (D-Prince George’s), who were reelected by a unanimous vote Wednesday of the Senate Democratic Caucus, according to a press release from Ferguson’s office.

The biggest change was in the Senate Executive Nominations Committee, where last year’s chairman, Sen. Clarence Lam (D-Howard and Anne Arundel) was moved out, replaced by Sen. Benjamin Brooks (D-Baltimore County). Lam, who had the misfortune of getting out, loudly, in support of redistricting just as Ferguson and the rest of the Senate were moving toward opposing, keeps his seat on the Finance Committee.

The only other standing committee chair to move is Sen. Shelly Hettleman (D-Baltimore County), who leaves the Rules Committee to become chair of Budget and Taxation’s Public Safety, Transportation and Environment Subcommittee in place of former Sen. Michael Jackson, who left the Senate to become superintendent of the Maryland State Police. Sen. Katie Fry Hester (D-Howard and Montgomery) takes over Rules.

Sen. Karen Lewis Young (D-Frederick) takes over as chair of Budget and Taxation’s Pensions Subcommittee, which had been held by Hettleman. Additionally, Augustine will fill Jackson’s seat on Budget and Tax, and Sen. Nick Charles (D-Prince George’s) takes over as vice chair of the Senate Democratic Caucus.

Sen. Kevin Harris (D-Prince George’s, Charles, and Calvert), who was just sworn in Wednesday, will join the Senate Committee on Education, Energy and the Environment.

“The Senate Democratic Caucus agenda will focus on growth, affordability, and protecting against attacks from the federal Administration in the 2026 Legislative Session,” Ferguson said in a statement released with the appointments. “We must give Marylanders the certainty and financial relief needed to navigate this avoidable chaos.”

Marc Schindler, former assistant secretary and chief of staff with the Maryland Department of Juvenile Services (DJS), will lead a national initiative to conduct research on children who died at juvenile facilities. The Forgotten Children Initiative at the Center for Youth Justice at Georgetown University’s McCourt School of Public Policy launches next month.

Schindler said in an email Wednesday that the first phase will focus on a burial site at the old House of Reformation and Instruction for Colored Children in southern Prince George’s County, a wooded area believed to hold the remains of at least 230 Black teens from the 19th and 20th centuries.

Work on that restoration project began with former DJS Secretary Vincent Schiraldi, who stepped down in June. Schindler, who also worked as an executive director of the Justice Policy Institute, first visited the site last year and later returned with department staff, a volunteer genealogist and some youth from the nearby Cheltenham detention center to look for headstones.

Schindler led a tour of the grounds with members of the Legislative Black Caucus of Maryland in September, when he said there are 230 known graves and possibly 100 more marked only with cinder blocks. But records from the time are missing and death certificates were not issued in most parts of the state until 1898.

DJS applied this summer for a $31,000 grant to the African American Heritage Preservation Program to work on restoring the wooded area.

“Marc brings energy, wide-ranging experience and vast knowledge of the youth justice field from a number of perspectives,” Michael Umpierre, director of Georgetown’s justice center, said in a statement. “Most importantly, he has the passion, expertise and drive needed to positively impact today’s justice system.”

The Black Caucus hopes to pass legislation in the 2026 General Assembly for a commission to investigate the deaths of the Cheltenham boys, and possibly identify other forgotten burial sites and cemeteries throughout the state.

The national effort by Georgetown’s justice center plans are to research unmarked graves, to not only tell the stories of youth buried there but also memorialize them.

“It may be easy to think that this is an initiative about the past, but the past is with us,” according to the justice center. “We need to ensure that all of our country’s forgotten children – whether laying under a cinderblock grave, or sitting in detention today – are treated with dignity and humanity.”

Gov. Wes Moore has appointed three new judges to the Baltimore City District Court and elevated an Anne Arundel County District Court judge to the county’s circuit court, “four exceptional legal minds who have dedicated their careers to upholding the law,” he said last week when making the appointments.

“Their collective experience — from public defense to prosecution and federal service — has prepared them well for the bench,” he said.

Moore named District Judge Sidney A. Butcher to a circuit court seat. First appointed to the bench in 2019, Butcher previously worked in the Medicaid Fraud Unit of the Maryland Attorney General’s Office, was in private practice and worked for a decade as a prosecutor in the Baltimore City State’s Attorney’s Office. He also served on the Anne Arundel County Board of Education. Butcher earned his law degree from the University of Kansas School of Law.

Moore appointed Elizabeth López, Noelle W. Newman and Otis W. Freeman to the Baltimore City District Court.

López has spent her entire legal career as a public defender, with 15 years in the Maryland Office of the Public Defender and the last four years in the Office of the Federal Public Defender, where she is a felony attorney supervisor, overseeing four attorneys. In Maryland, she created a model for the defense of children charged as adults. Earlier in her career, she represented juveniles and adults in criminal and civil commitment proceedings with the Defender Association in Seattle. She got her law degree from the University of St. Thomas School of Law.

Newman has served as counsel for Pessin Katz Law’s general litigation group since 2022, handling domestic relations matters, civil, and state and federal criminal defense. She spent 15 years before that at the Baltimore City State’s Attorney’s Office, rising to deputy state’s attorney in 2021. In district, juvenile, and circuit courts, she handled cases ranging from misdemeanors to complex felonies including sexual child abuse and homicides. Newman earned her law degree from the Catholic University of America, Columbus School of Law.

Freeman has been assistant chief counsel since 2o22 in the Baltimore Office of the Principal Legal Advisor in the Department of Homeland Security since 2022. Before that, Freeman spent four years with the Maryland Office of the Attorney General representing the Uninsured Employers’ Fund in workers’ compensation hearings. He spent seven years in the Baltimore City State’s Attorney’s Office, and began his legal career as a law clerk for the office’s homicide unit. He got his law degree from the University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law.
